newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Parole of journalist seen as HK morale-booster.
newsitem.headline: Parole of journalist seen as HK morale-booster.

text.p: Beijing's unexpected release of Hong Kong journalist Xi Yang was intended to boost morale in the British colony during the countdown to the handover, newspapers said on Sunday.

"The official reason for unconditional release -- because he showed 'signs of repentance' -- smacks of a face-saving excuse for the communist authorities to right their wrongs," political commentator Chris Yeung wrote in the English-language South China Morning Post.
Xi was released on parole on Saturday, three years into his 12 year prison sentence for stealing state secrets.
Hong Kong's Democratic Party said the handover factor was the most logical reason behind China's decision to release Yang.
"Out of all the possible reasons behind the decision, the handover factor is the most understandable," party vice chairman Yeung Sam said.

Xi's release comes against a backdrop of outrage in the territory over Beijing's plans to roll back civil liberties in Hong Kong after the handover. Pro-democracy activists have staged protests during the past week over the plans.
China insists the alterations would not weaken human rights protections in the territory after the handover.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.

Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, welcomed Xi's release in a statement, saying it was good that he could be reunited with his family ahead of the Chinese New Year season that starts early next month.
"I am pleased he can join his family for Lunar New Year," the statement said.
His office dismissed widespread speculation in Hong Kong that the chief executive-designate was behind the release.
The Hong Kong Journalists Association also called Xi's parole a positive signal.
"At the eve of handover of Hong Kong sovereignty, we appreciate that the Beijing authority has sent a positive signal to Hong Kong," it said in a statement on Sunday.
"We always believed Xi Yang was doing his job as a professional journalist and his imprisonment was unwarranted."
China jailed Xi, now 40, for 12 years in March 1994 on charges of stealing state secrets about internal policies on interest rates and gold.
The severity of the sentence shocked Hong Kong reporters, already pessimistic about the prospects for a free press after the handover and triggered protests in the British colony.
"We hope that the Beijing government would have more understanding and flexibility in responding to Hong Kong journalists covering news in mainland China," the journalists association said.
But Yeung of the South China Morning Post said Beijing would have to go further to shore up confidence in Hong Kong.

"While senior Beijing leaders may have wanted to create a more relaxed atmosphere in the 157 days to the changeover by allowing Xi to return home, Beijing will have to do far more to dispel fears that civil liberties are about to be curtailed," he said.
